planting.note: Float fragments in a sunny, still, nutrient-rich pond or stock tank without soil; overwinters as dense turions that sink to the bottom and re-float in spring.

directions: The widespread temperate North American bladderwort, distinct from the showier tropical Utricularia already in the collection, forming dense submerged masses in ponds, lakes, and slow streams across most of the continent. It survives winter as turions that drop to the substrate when water cools, re-floating and resuming growth in spring. Site it in a contained water feature, since it spreads vigorously in nutrient-rich water and can become weedy if released into open waterways.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Float a rosette in rainwater or pond water, never chlorinated tap water, in a small sunny tub or trough; thin periodically since it propagates readily from fragments.

directions: A smaller lookalike of the already-present Utricularia inflata, distinguished by cylindrical rather than tapered floats and racemes of just one to five flowers instead of nine to fourteen, making it the better choice for a smaller tub or trough water feature. It is native across the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plain from Texas to New England in acidic, tannin-stained bog ponds. Keep it in rainwater or pond water and thin periodically as it spreads from fragments.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Plant Directory
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Anchor divisions into substrate in a genuinely deep, clean, still water feature at least 2 feet deep; source nursery divisions only, never wild-collected material.

directions: A large, rhizome-affixed bladderwort of deep limesink ponds and Carolina-bay-type lakes from the Florida panhandle and southwest Georgia north into the Carolinas. Unlike most Utricularia in the collection it anchors into substrate rather than free-floating, so it needs a genuinely deep, clean, still water feature rather than a shallow bog tray. It is secure globally but imperiled in parts of its range, so source nursery divisions only.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Introduce a free-floating rosette into a large, sunny, nutrient-rich pond margin rather than a peat-based bog tray; thrives in calcareous or richly organic standing water.

directions: A large, free-floating bladderwort native from North Carolina west to Texas and south to Miami-Dade, thriving in calcareous or richly organic, permanently wet swamps and marshes. It wants full sun and nutrient-rich water, making it a good match for a large Gulf Coast pond margin rather than a peat-based tray. Its bright yellow summer and fall flowers are a genuine pollinator draw distinct from the other Utricularia species already in the collection.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)
